column3: NASB follows the critical text without the Textus Receptus words “who walk not according to the flesh but according to the Spirit.”
NASB follows the critical text (“you”).
NASB restructures the verse as “what the Law could not do … God did”; “flesh of sin” is rendered “sinful flesh,” and “for sin” is “as an offering for sin.”
NASB renders “righteousness” as “requirement.”
NASB renders “mind” as “set their minds on.”
NASB renders “the mind of the flesh” as “the mind set on the flesh.”
NASB renders “hostility” as “hostile” and adds “to do so.”
Close to the Greek.
NASB renders “he is not of Him” as “he does not belong to Him.”
NASB renders “the Spirit is life” as “the spirit is alive” and adds “though … yet.”
NASB reads “Christ Jesus,” including “Jesus,” which the critical text lacks; it follows the critical text with “through His Spirit who indwells you.”
NASB renders “debtors” as “under obligation.”
NASB renders “you are about to die” as “you must die.”
Close to the Greek.
NASB renders “bondage” as “slavery,” adds “leading,” and has “a spirit” in lowercase for adoption.
Close to the Greek.
NASB renders “joint-heirs” as “fellow heirs.”
NASB renders “not comparable” as “not worthy to be compared.”
NASB renders “earnest expectation” as “anxious longing” and “awaits” as “waits eagerly for.”
NASB renders “not willingly” as “not of its own will.”
NASB renders “the bondage of decay” as “its slavery to corruption.”
NASB renders “travails together” as “suffers the pains of childbirth together.”
NASB adds “eagerly” and “our.”
NASB follows the critical text; “we were saved” is rendered “we have been saved.”
NASB renders “patience” as “perseverance” and adds “eagerly.”
NASB follows the critical text (“weakness”); “for us” renders the compound verb, since the critical text lacks the Textus Receptus “for us.” “Inexpressible” is rendered “too deep for words.”
NASB renders “mindset” as “mind” and adds “the will of.”
NASB follows the reading with “God” as subject (“God causes all things to work together”), found in some manuscripts.
NASB renders “brothers” as “brethren.”
Close to the Greek.
